opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is pretty simple: training is a one-time cost, and inference is a recurring cost that scales with usage.

When you train a model, you spend a big chunk of compute up front. It might be weeks or months on a large cluster, and it's very visible, so people talk about it a lot. But once that model is deployed, every single user request, every token generated, every API call, consumes compute. If the model is successful, it's serving millions of people, many times a day, for months or even years. Integrate that over the model's lifetime and the inference bill very quickly passes the training bill, often by a large multiple.

A few trends make this even more pronounced. First, adoption. AI is moving from demos into actual products and enterprise workflows, so the request volume keeps going up. Second, the way we use models is changing. With reasoning models and agents, a single user task may involve many steps, long chains of thought, tool calls, and retries. The tokens per task have gone up dramatically, and all of that is inference. Third, the industry has found that you can trade inference compute for quality, which people call test-time scaling. So there's a direct incentive to spend more at inference time.

There's also an economic point. Training cost is something only a handful of frontier labs pay at the largest scale. Inference cost is paid by everyone building on top of these models, every company and every application. So in aggregate, across the whole industry, inference is where most of the compute dollars end up flowing.

That's why I think the infrastructure problem is shifting. It used to be "how do we train the biggest model." Now, more and more, it's "how do we serve these models efficiently, reliably, and cheaply at scale." That covers better kernels, quantization, batching, scheduling across heterogeneous hardware, and squeezing utilization out of GPUs. A 2x improvement in inference efficiency, applied over the whole lifetime of a widely used model, is worth far more than a similar saving on the training run.

r001.rationale: The response does not explain that finding a model useless leads to curtailing further training.

r002.rationale: It explains that a successful, widely used model incurs recurring inference costs that accumulate over its lifetime and can quickly exceed its upfront training cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The simplest way I think about it is that training is a one-time cost, and inference is a recurring cost. You train a model once, maybe a few times with some iterations, and that's a big check you write up front. But once that model is good enough to be useful, it starts serving requests, and it serves them every second, every day, for as long as people find value in it. That's the part that compounds.

Think about any successful product. The whole point of building it is that lots of people use it, and use it repeatedly. If a model is actually good, usage grows, and every one of those queries costs compute. So if you add up the cost of every token generated over the lifetime of a widely used model, that number dwarfs what it took to train it. If it doesn't, honestly, that's a sign the model wasn't very successful, because nobody used it enough.

There's also a structural reason. Training is something you can plan and optimize as a single large job on a dedicated cluster. Inference is messy. It's latency sensitive, it's bursty, you have to provision for peak traffic, you often can't batch as efficiently, and you're running it across many regions to be close to users. So the per-unit economics of inference are inherently harder, and that's where a lot of the engineering effort in the industry is now going, things like quantization, better serving stacks, speculative decoding, cheaper hardware. That's exactly why we focused on it at Lepton.

And one more thing I'd add. As models get better and cheaper to run, people find more things to do with them, so demand goes up faster than cost per token comes down. That's a classic Jevons kind of dynamic. So even as inference gets more efficient, total inference spend keeps growing. Training will always be a big, visible number, but over the life of a model, inference is where the money really goes.

r001.rationale: The response says an unsuccessful model would not get enough use, but does not explain that this leads to curtailing further training.

r002.rationale: It explains that a useful, widely used model accumulates inference costs with every query over time, eventually dwarfing its training cost.

astra-6.text:
Training is a large upfront expense, but inference is a recurring expense. You train a model, then potentially serve it to millions of users, answering requests every day. Each request costs much less than a training run, but over the model’s lifetime, those requests add up.

So it depends on how much the model is used. If you train a model and hardly anyone uses it, training will dominate. But for a successful product deployed at scale, the cumulative computation for inference can exceed what you spent on training. That’s why inference efficiency matters so much: even a small reduction in cost per request becomes significant when you multiply it by the total usage.

r001.rationale: The response says training may dominate if a model is hardly used, but does not explain that finding a model useless leads to curtailing further training.

r002.rationale: It explains that a useful model deployed at scale accumulates enough inference computation for inference costs to exceed training costs.

sol-6.1.text:
Training is a big upfront investment, but inference is a recurring cost. You train a model, and then every time someone uses it, you spend compute to generate a response. If the model becomes popular, you’re serving those requests continuously, potentially for years.

So it depends on usage. A model that nobody uses may cost more to train than to serve. But for a successful model, the accumulated volume of inference can far exceed the compute spent on training. That’s why inference efficiency matters so much: even a small reduction in cost per request becomes significant when you multiply it across all those requests.

r001.rationale: The response says an unused model may cost more to train than to serve, but does not explain that finding it useless leads to curtailing further training.

r002.rationale: It explains that a successful, popular model’s accumulated inference costs can far exceed its training compute.
